78: The dough is the heart of a Neapolitan-style pizza shop, so write its recipe in numbers, not adjectives. Work in grams and baker's percentages, the way the trade does: 00 flour at 100%, water, salt and fresh or dry yeast as a percentage of the flour, and a hydration you set after testing your own flour and oven. A common starting range for this style is about 58-65% hydration (the traditional ratios in the calculator sit at 55-62%), with salt and yeast adjusted to your fermentation time. A same-day dough and a cold-fermented dough (a biga, a poolish or another preferment) behave differently, so pick one method, write it down and keep it. Mix, rest, then ball the dough by hand into 250 g (8.8 oz) dough balls, let them proof at room temperature or cold-ferment them in dough boxes, and use them within the window your written procedure sets. Stretch by hand, no rolling pin, to a pie of up to about 14 in (35 cm) with a thin center and a soft cornicione, and bake for 60-90 seconds at about 900 °F (480 °C) on the oven floor. If dough balls or cut toppings sit out of refrigeration, put time as a public health control (TPHC) in writing: the Food Code (3-501.19) allows up to 4 hours or up to 6 hours if you start at 41 °F or below and never go above 70 °F, with marked start and discard times. For raw dough itself, ask your health department how it classifies it. The calculator in this kit has two inputs: grams of ingredients and baker's percentages. It does not set your fermentation times; that is your recipe. Cost every pizza, not just the Margherita: fior di latte, mozzarella di bufala (DOP), burrata and imported cured meats push the food cost per pizza up fast.
79: The oven is the big decision, and you should make it before you sign the lease. The case uses a Neapolitan wood-fired dome oven, 47-51 in (120-130 cm), UL 2162-listed, for {{inv_horno}}. Published prices vary a lot: Forno Bravo lists commercial models from $12,950, and many Italian and American makers (Marra Forni, for example) publish no price, so ask for a quote that includes installation and delivery. Add the flue, spark arrestor and insulated hearth pad, {{inv_chimenea}}, and budget firewood as a fixed cost: {{lena_ano}} a year. You burn it by the hour the oven is lit, not by the pizza, and it must be dry, untreated hardwood (oak, ash, maple or fruitwood). A gas oven needs a licensed gas contractor and its fuel use is fixed too, but be aware that an electric oven never qualifies for VPN certification, and a gas oven only where wood burning is forbidden and documented. Neither one automatically frees you from a hood or from a ventilation review: ask your fire marshal in writing.
80: Size production for your busiest Saturday, not for the average day. The case averages {{clientes_dia}} covers a day and {{ventas_dia}} in sales per opening day, and a six-pizza oven at 90 seconds a pie can bake well over a hundred pizzas an hour in theory, so the oven is rarely the limit: the stretcher's hands are. A 60-quart spiral mixer covers a busy Saturday in two batches. The rest of the equipment list is short: spiral mixer {{inv_amasadora}}, pizza prep table {{inv_mesa_fria}}, walk-in, reach-ins and dough-ball cabinets {{inv_frio}}, and the Type I hood and support line for the fryer and range {{inv_campana}}. Ask for quotes with installation and lead times, because prices change by brand.
81: There is a reasoned alternative, outside the Excel: an electric oven instead of wood. You skip the wood-fired oven ({{inv_horno}}), the flue and the spark arrestor ({{inv_chimenea}}), and the firewood ({{lena_ano}} a year), and you pay instead for a high-power electric oven and a bigger electrical service. In exchange you give up the VPN certification (the AVPN does not accept electric ovens), although you can still call your pizza Neapolitan-style, and you may still need a hood and exhaust for the fumes. If your city does not allow wood smoke, this can be your way out; if it does, compare both budgets with real quotes before you decide.
82: The case opens Tuesday through Sunday, with lunch from 11:30 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. and dinner from 5:00 to 10:00 p.m., and closes on Mondays, on the main holidays (Thanksgiving, Christmas, New Year's Day and July 4) and for two weeks in January. Food safety rests on your written HACCP-based food safety plan: log dough ball times and temperatures, hold mozzarella and cut tomatoes at 41 °F or below, and send food out in boxes that hold the temperature of what goes in them. Have the hood and flue cleaned on the schedule NFPA 96 and your fire marshal require, and budget for oven maintenance. Utilities average {{suministros_mes}} a month: check the electrical and gas service of the space before you sign.
85: The team in the case is short and designed so that nobody is irreplaceable. You are the head pizzaiolo and the GM: dough, the oven on the busy shift, ordering and management. The case pays you a modest wage, below the national median for food service managers, and anything above that is a draw from net profit; ask your accountant how your LLC is taxed. Beside you there is a second pizzaiolo who works the oven and the stretching and can also make the dough, a prep and dough cook, a front-of-house lead who runs the floor and the beer and wine bar all year, part-time servers on dinners and weekends, and a weekend runner.
86: With relief coverage for vacations and days off, the schedule adds up to {{plantilla_puestos}} people, equal to {{plantilla_jornadas}} full-time equivalents, and labor costs {{personal_a1}} in year 1 including employer payroll taxes of {{cargas_pct}}: {{personal_pct}} of sales. It is the biggest expense of the business, bigger than rent ({{ocupacion_anual}}, or {{ocupacion_pct}} of sales). The schedule covers {{cobertura_horas}} of the hours the shop needs: tight, with little room for sick days. The weekend runner handles the dining room, the patio, pickup and the delivery tablet, with no drivers of your own, and a Saturday night takes about five people. Headcount grows by hiring people, not by a percentage, so add each new hire in the Staffing tab.
87: Pay every employee at least the highest of the federal minimum wage ($7.25 an hour, according to the Department of Labor), your state's and your city's, and remember that many states and cities are well above it. The case budgets at least $15 an hour and does not model a tip credit. Hourly employees get overtime above 40 hours a week under the FLSA. Give every hire an offer letter in writing, complete Form I-9 and Form W-4 on day one, and keep accurate time records. Your accountant or payroll provider confirms which state and local rules apply to you.
88: One warning: never replace payroll staff with 1099 contractors who work your schedule under your direction. That is misclassification, and the IRS, the Department of Labor and your state can all come after you for back taxes and penalties. If you hire anyone under 18, the federal and state rules limit their hours and ban some equipment, including some dough mixers and slicers, so check with the Department of Labor and your state before you schedule them. And think about the single-pizzaiolo risk: it is not a saving, it is a risk. If the only person who masters the oven calls in sick, the shop closes, so a second pizzaiolo who can also make the dough is the best insurance you will ever pay for.
89: If you ever want your own drivers, they are W-2 employees, not independent contractors, and you need hired and non-owned auto liability on top of your general policy; check your state for the details. That is why the case sells through third-party delivery marketplaces instead, capped at {{plataforma_pct}} of sales with a commission of {{comision_pct}} on those orders, and with no drivers of its own. Do the math before you change that: a part-time driver's wages, payroll taxes, extra auto insurance and fuel or mileage against the marketplace commission on the same orders. Your own drivers only pay off with a high delivery volume or a short, dense delivery zone, and they cost you the marketplace's storefront.
90: Train the team before you open. Every person who handles food needs a food handler card where your state or county requires one, and at least one person in charge needs the Certified Food Protection Manager (CFPM) certification under Food Code 2-102.12, if your jurisdiction has adopted it. Training should cover dough and cheese temperatures, the 9 major allergens and cross-contact. Separately, you need pizzaiolo training: dough, fire and peel. Then cover the OSHA basics: burns from the oven, cuts, lifting firewood and sacks of flour, heat and smoke are the typical accidents in this kitchen. Schedule a short refresher whenever someone new joins, because what is not repeated is forgotten.
93: To open, you need {{necesidad_caja}} in cash. Startup costs without working capital come to {{capex}}: build-out, oven, equipment and launch, plus a security deposit, {{meses_alquiler_previo}} months of rent paid before you open, and a contingency. Working capital adds {{fondo_maniobra}}. You fund it with {{fondos_propios}} of your own money ({{aportacion_pct}} of the cash needed) and a loan of {{prestamo}} at {{tipo_prestamo}} (nominal, not APR) over {{plazo_prestamo}} years, a typical SBA 7(a) structure, with an annual payment of {{cuota_anual}}. Sales tax you pay on purchases is part of the cost (the workbook recovers none); exemptions such as resale certificates depend on your state, so confirm them with your accountant.
94: The three-year profit and loss projects revenue, excluding sales tax, of {{ventas_a1}}, {{ventas_a2}} and {{ventas_a3}}. Gross margin in year 1 is {{margen_bruto_pct}}, after all the variable costs: cost of goods ({{cogs_pct}} of sales), disposables, delivery marketplace fees, card processing and contingency. Labor adds up to {{personal_a1}}, rent to {{ocupacion_anual}} ({{ocupacion_pct}} of sales) and marketing to {{marketing_anual}}. EBITDA, earnings before depreciation, interest and taxes, is {{ebitda_a1}}, or {{ebitda_pct_a1}} of sales. Net profit is {{resultado_neto_a1}}, {{resultado_neto_a2}} and {{resultado_neto_a3}}; the net margin in year 1 is {{margen_neto_a1}}, after an effective income tax rate of {{impuesto_beneficios}}. The example applies it as if the business paid corporate income tax (an LLC can elect it); as a pass-through, set the rate to 0 on "0. Assumptions" and budget your personal tax. How your business is actually taxed depends on whether you run it as an LLC, an S corp or something else, so confirm that with your CPA. It is an honest figure: the 15-25% net margins that circulate online for pizza shops do not hold up with a fully staffed, legal team, and a 2026 report in PMQ Pizza Magazine quotes an independent operator at 2% to 3%.
95: Growth is the one the Excel applies: covers rise {{crecimiento_a2}} in year 2 and {{crecimiento_a3}} in year 3, from {{clientes_dia}} to {{clientes_a2}} and {{clientes_a3}} a day, with the same average check of {{ticket}} excluding sales tax, and staff grows by hiring people, not by a percentage. Sales are about {{comida_pct}} food and {{bebida_pct}} beverages (beer, wine, soft drinks and coffee), with a cost of goods of {{food_cost_comida}} on food and {{food_cost_bebida}} on beverages. The workbook uses one example sales tax rate of {{sales_tax}} and keeps it out of revenue: you collect it from guests and remit it to the state. Rates, and whether take-out is taxed differently from dine-in, vary by state and city, so check with your state revenue department.
96: Accounting break-even is {{equilibrio_clientes_dia}} covers a day, or {{equilibrio_ventas}} a year in revenue. Cash break-even, which counts loan payments and leaves out depreciation, is {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} covers a day, or {{equilibrio_caja_ventas}}, and leaves a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}} over the plan. The cash figure is the one to watch, because it is the one that pays the bank. If you negotiate an interest-only period, the margin will look better until principal payments start, so check the later years in the workbook before you celebrate. The {{clientes_dia}} covers a day on {{aforo}} indoor seats imply {{rotaciones_dia}} seat turns a day, but covers include guests who take the pizza home or have it delivered and never sit at a table.
97: The cash flow numbers the months from 1 to 12, and Month 1 is September. Sales start below full pace and reach it in 4 months, around the holidays, which means Christmas finds you with guests and January and February (Months 5 and 6) arrive with your reserve intact. The lowest cash balance, {{saldo_minimo}}, comes in month {{mes_saldo_minimo}}. Sales tax is remitted on your state's schedule; the workbook assumes you file quarterly, and if your state requires monthly filing, move the payments accordingly. Remember the tax is the guests' money, not yours, and keep it out of your working capital.
98: The lowest DSCR, or debt service coverage ratio, is {{dscr_min}}, and in year 1 it is {{dscr_a1}}: the business covers its debt with room to spare over the {{dscr_objetivo}} that lenders usually look for. That is a typical guideline, not a rule, and a bank will still want to see your sales plan. Payback, in years and before debt, is {{payback}} counting working capital, and {{payback_capex}} counting startup costs alone. This is not a fast-payback investment; it is a craft business that pays you a modest salary and returns the capital with patience.
99: The pessimistic scenario is a weak year: {{pesimista_clientes}} covers a day at an average check of {{pesimista_ticket}} over {{pesimista_dias}} days gives sales of {{pesimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}. In the optimistic one, {{optimista_clientes}} covers at {{optimista_ticket}} over {{optimista_dias}} days give sales of {{optimista_ventas}} and a pre-tax result of {{optimista_resultado}}. The distance between the two separates a good year from a bad one. And remember: the Excel rules, and if you change a green cell, this document stays behind.
102: Most owners open as an LLC, which you file with your state, and many add an operating agreement; talk to your CPA about LLC versus S corp taxation. Then get an EIN from the IRS and register for a sales tax permit with your state. In the US, requirements stack in layers: federal, state, county and city, and each one has its own forms. Apply for the city or county business license and, before you sign anything, run a zoning check on the exact address. Submit your plans for plan review with the health department (Food Code 8-201.11 asks for plans before construction or remodeling), then get your building permit and, at the end, the certificate of occupancy. The workbook uses an example sales tax of {{sales_tax}}, a single rate; yours depends on the state and city.
103: A wood-fired oven falls under NFPA 96, chapter 14, on solid fuel cooking: a dedicated exhaust that serves only solid-fuel appliances, a spark arrestor, ashes removed at least once a day into a metal container, and fuel stored away from the oven. Chapter numbers vary by edition, so check which one your jurisdiction adopted. Buy an oven that is UL 2162-listed. Oregon's Statewide Code Interpretation 15-01 is an example of an authority having jurisdiction (AHJ) that does not require a Type I hood over a listed refractory oven with the manufacturer's chimney connection, but it applies only in Oregon. Your city decides for you, so ask the fire marshal in writing: hood? suppression? UL 2162 file number? Never assume the hood is optional. The case budgets the flue and spark arrestor at {{inv_chimenea}} and a Type I hood for the support line (fryer and range) at {{inv_campana}}.
104: Before opening you need a health permit and a pre-opening inspection, after the plan review above. At least one person in charge should hold a Certified Food Protection Manager (CFPM) certificate (Food Code 2-102.12), and food handler cards depend on your state or county. Fior di latte and other fresh mozzarella, cooked ham, raw sausage and cut tomatoes are TCS foods (some dry-cured meats are not: check the label), so hold them at 41 °F or below, or at 135 °F or above if hot. If anything sits out, use a written TPHC procedure (Food Code 3-501.19): up to 4 hours, or up to 6 hours if you start at 41 °F or below and never go above 70 °F, with the hours marked. For the dough balls, the Food Code gives no specific rule; ask your regulator how they classify them, and build your HACCP-based food safety plan around the answer. A licensed gas contractor installs any gas line, and your city will inspect it.
105: Tell guests about allergens: the US recognizes 9 major allergens, including sesame (FASTER Act, effective January 1, 2023). On a pizza menu, wheat and milk are always present, and eggs, tree nuts, soy and sesame show up in desserts, pestos, sauces and starters. Shared peels and benches mean cross-contact, so train for it. Do not promise "gluten-free": under 21 CFR 101.91 the claim means less than 20 ppm of gluten, and flour in the air makes that impossible to guarantee without a protocol and testing. Offer "gluten-friendly, ask your server" with a clear notice instead. Check your state and city for other required public notices as well, such as consumer advisories and posting rules.
106: If you serve beer and wine, you need a license from your state's alcohol beverage control (ABC) agency plus local approval. In a state without a quota, the case budgets about $3,000 for the license and sits inside the {{inv_proyecto}} project line; in a state with quotas it can cost much more, so ask your ABC. It often takes 3 to 12 months, so write a contingency into your lease: you should be able to walk away or pay reduced rent if the license is delayed. Your insurance, budgeted at {{seguros_anual}} a year in the case, should combine general liability with liquor liability and property coverage that accounts for open flame; workers' compensation is budgeted in the payroll taxes. Train staff in responsible alcohol service. Playing recorded music in the dining room needs licenses from ASCAP, BMI and SESAC, and some cities have packaging ordinances for take-out containers, so ask the city before you order boxes.
107: Now, the name on your menu. You can write "Neapolitan-style" freely: we found no federal US rule that restricts it. What you cannot do is say "VPN-certified" unless you hold the certificate from the AVPN, the private Naples association, whose US program requires an open shop, a wood-fired dome oven (gas only where wood is banned), flour 00 or 0 and a pizza up to about 14 in (35 cm); the EU's own rule, Regulation (EU) 97/2010, has no force in the US. Claiming a seal you do not hold is misleading advertising. The case menu says "Margherita", "Marinara" and "Diavola", plus "wood-fired Neapolitan-style". If you hire your own drivers, they are W-2 employees with hired and non-owned auto coverage, and your marketplace contracts should be read line by line.
108: Selling pizza from your home kitchen is another matter. There is no federal rule, and state cottage food laws cover low-risk products; a pizza with cheese is a TCS food, so this plan assumes a permitted shop, and you should check your state before you try anything else. This section lists what we can state with confidence; for everything else, check with your accountant, your city or the health inspector before you decide. A note for UK readers: register your food business with your local council at least 28 days before you open, expect a Food Hygiene Rating of 0 to 5 (FHIS in Scotland), VAT at 20% on hot food and on food eaten in, 14 allergens to declare, a smoke control area check with Environmental Health for the wood-fired oven, and a premises plus a personal licence if you sell alcohol.
111: The conclusion is that a pizza shop of this size is viable, but demanding. With {{clientes_dia}} covers a day at an average check of {{ticket}} excluding sales tax, year 1 leaves a net profit of {{resultado_neto_a1}} and a cash margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}}. The lowest DSCR is {{dscr_min}}, the lowest cash balance is {{saldo_minimo}} in month {{mes_saldo_minimo}} and the payback, in years and before debt, is {{payback}}. Check the later years in the workbook, once any interest-only period ends and you repay principal. This is not a business to open with tight capital.
112: The first risk, and the most expensive, is signing a lease for a space where the exhaust cannot reach the roof. Without a dedicated flue there is no wood-fired oven, and an electric one does not automatically free you from a hood either: ask the fire marshal in writing before you sign the lease. The second is calling your pizza "VPN-certified" without the AVPN certificate, which exposes you to taking it off the menu, the website and the marketplace listing. Say "Neapolitan-style" and name each pizza: Margherita, Marinara, Diavola. The third is costing only the Margherita: with mozzarella di bufala, burrata or imported cured meats, your best seller can run far above the plan's food cost, and on marketplace orders the commission comes out of the price on top. Cost every pizza on the menu with the calculator in this kit.
113: The fourth is joining the marketplaces without doing the math: between the commission, the promotions and the packaging, the cash register eats the margin. That is why the case caps them at {{plataforma_pct}} of sales and measures every order. The fifth is underestimating firewood and oven maintenance: firewood alone is {{lena_ano}} a year, and wet or treated wood fouls the oven, the smoke and the pizza. Buy dry, untreated wood and schedule the cleaning. The sixth is dough without a protocol: leftover dough balls after a slow Saturday and missing dough balls on a full one. With times and temperatures logged, and a batch sized on the day's sales, you avoid both.
114: The seventh is promising "gluten-free" with flour in the air; it takes a protocol and testing. The eighth is skipping the local rules on required public notices and packaging, which a quick call to your city settles. And one risk decides the plan: the cash of years 2 and 3. With a margin of safety of {{holgura_caja_pct}} in the case, there is not much room. Track covers every month against the {{equilibrio_caja_clientes_dia}} covers a day you need at cash break-even, and keep in mind that the pessimistic scenario closes with a pre-tax result of {{pesimista_resultado}}.
115: The ninth is the single pizzaiolo: one sick day closes the shop, so train a second person early who can make the dough and run the oven. The tenth is hiring your own drivers as 1099 contractors, which is misclassification: if you deliver yourself, use W-2 employees, and run the numbers against the marketplace first. The eleventh is treating the beer and wine license as an afterthought, when it can take 3 to 12 months. None of these is expensive to avoid if you see it in time, and all of them are expensive if you find out after opening. Review these points with your accountant and your team before you open, and go back to them after three months, when the daily work piles up and the important things get pushed back.
116: The action plan has six phases and 80 tasks in the checklist that comes with the kit. Phase 1 is setup and taxes, with 12 tasks. Phase 2, site, hood and permits, has 15. Phase 3, kitchen, oven and health, has 14. Phase 4, staff and safety, has 13. Phase 5, menu, brand and delivery, has 13. And phase 6, opening and the first 90 days, has 13. Follow the order: the zoning check and the fire marshal's answer on the hood and flue, and the oven decision, come before you sign the lease, and the beer and wine license application goes in as soon as you do. Check off each task when you close it, and if one slips, see what depends on it before you move the opening date.
117: The next step is to fill in the Excel with your own numbers: your real rent, your average check, your covers, your loan, your staff and your opening calendar. Change only the green cells; this document reflects the example case, and yours is set by your spreadsheet. Then cost your whole menu with the dough and food cost calculator, not just the Margherita. With your own data in front of you, come back to this section and check what is left in cash in years 2 and 3 if the year turns out like the pessimistic scenario. If the cash holds up, you have a solid plan to take to the bank; if not, adjust the investment, the staffing or the calendar before you sign anything.
